newsitem.title: DENMARK: East Asiatic sees reasonable 1997 progress.
newsitem.headline: East Asiatic sees reasonable 1997 progress.

text.p: Danish wholesale, consumer goods and graphics group East Asiatic(EAC) posted 1996 pre-tax and extraordinary items profits 59 percent up on 1995 and forecast "reasonably better" 1997 operating profits.
"East Asiatic expects turnover growth to continue this year," the company said in a statement accompanying its 1996 result.
"Our strategies of consolidating EAC's market position are seen providing a reasonable advance in operating profits in 1997," it said.

EAC profits before tax and extraordinary items rose in 1996 to 343 million crowns from the previous year's 216 million crown surplus, with net profits falling to 201 million crowns from 1995's 338 million crowns.
Operating profits for last year were 402 million crowns against 422 in 1995.
EAC's pre-tax and extraordinary items profit for 1996 was short of average analyst expectations of 357 million crowns.
"The 1997 result before tax and extraordinary items will however only partially reflect better operating profits," EAC said.

It said currency and securities market trends during the year would play a major role in the group's overall performance, adding that currency factors, notably the U.S. dollar and Venezuelan Bolivar, had had a positive effect since the new year.

EAC said it expected "reasonable" progress in its core activities - EAC Graphics, EAC Consumer Products and EAC Foods - as well as in ancillary activities. The vast bulk of EAC's former shipping activity was divested in January.

It described prospects for EAC Graphics as positive and said that a rationalisation and efficiency drive was being given high priority by the division, although its marketing of Kodak products was not scheduled to start until this year.
EAC said its marketing of Kodak products would be implemented in all its African and Asian markets in 1998.

EAC Consumer Products was seen making marked progress this year, with major wholesaling and distribution projects in the Philippines, but setting up costs in China were still expected to be loss-making, although to a lesser extent than in 1996, it said.
It said it saw EAC Foods still being hit by low consumption in early 1997 but was optimistic about a gradual improvement in sales for the unit later on in the year.
The EAC share had fallen eight crowns to 151 by 1305 gmt.
